how_to_obtain.command: gitlab-rake gitlab:env:info 2>/dev/null | grep 'GitLab information' -A5 || gitea --version || forgejo --version
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output such as: 'GitLab 16.2.3' or 'Gitea Version: 1.20.4', which can then be checked against CVE databases.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use Trivy to scan the running container image or installed package for known CVEs affecting the Git platform version.
how_to_obtain.command: trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL gitlab/gitlab-ce:latest 2>/dev/null || trivy fs --severity HIGH,CRITICAL /opt/gitea/
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A table listing CVE IDs, severity, affected package, and fixed version. Empty output indicates no known CVEs.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the GitLab version API endpoint and cross-reference the returned version against the GitLab security releases page (https://about.gitlab.com/releases/categories/releases/) for listed CVEs.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON object like: {"version": "16.2.3-ee", "revision": "abc1234"}, which should be compared against the GitLab security advisories page.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use Grype to scan the installed binary or package database for CVEs affecting the Git service.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines listing CVE IDs and affected components. No output indicates no known fixable CVEs detected.

typical_values: true (common in organizations without automated version monitoring)

option_description: Indicates whether a formal patch management policy or automated update process is in place for the Git platform, ensuring timely application of security patches. This encompasses documented procedures, scheduled patching windows, version monitoring tooling, and designated responsibility.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'outdated_platform_version_without_patch_management' when patch_management_policy_exists is false AND days_since_last_version_update >= 90. Without a patch management policy, organizations run known-vulnerable versions indefinitely, giving attackers a persistent exploitation window against a service that aggregates all source code, secrets, and CI/CD pipeline definitions.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the platform owner or infrastructure team to determine whether a documented patch management policy exists. Request evidence of the policy document, patch schedule, and the process for monitoring vendor security advisories.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A documented policy with named owner, review cadence, patching SLA (e.g., critical CVEs patched within 14 days), and evidence of recent patch activity such as changelog or ticket records.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for automated update tooling or cron jobs on the host that manage platform version updates.
how_to_obtain.command: crontab -l 2>/dev/null; ls /etc/cron.d/ | grep -i 'gitlab\|gitea\|update\|patch'; systemctl list-timers | grep -i 'gitlab\|gitea\|update'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Scheduled cron entries or systemd timers referencing update scripts or package managers indicate automated patching. Absence of any output suggests manual-only updates.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for package manager auto-update configurations that include the Git platform package.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: APT: 'APT::Periodic::Unattended-Upgrade "1";' or DNF: 'apply_updates = yes' confirms automated patching is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review package manager or deployment logs to determine how frequently the platform has been updated, providing evidence of an active patch process.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log entries showing regular upgrade activity with recent dates. Large gaps between upgrade events suggest absence of a formal patch process.

typical_values: true (expected in mature engineering organizations with documented runbooks)

option_description: The number of days elapsed since the Git platform was last updated to a new release or patch version. This is calculated from the installed version's release date or the date the package was last upgraded on the host.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires 'outdated_platform_version_without_patch_management' when patch_management_policy_exists is false AND days_since_last_version_update >= 90. Ninety days without an update in a platform that publishes monthly security releases is a strong indicator that known-exploitable vulnerabilities are present. Extended staleness (>180 days) on a high-value target like a Git service significantly increases the probability that publicly available exploit code exists for the running version.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the installed package's installation or upgrade timestamp using the package manager.
how_to_obtain.command:
stat --format='%y' $(which gitlab-ctl 2>/dev/null || which gitea 2>/dev/null) | awk '{print $1}'; rpm -q --queryformat '%{INSTALLTIME:date}
' gitlab-ee 2>/dev/null || dpkg-query -l gitlab-ee 2>/dev/null | grep '^ii'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A timestamp such as '2024-03-15' indicating when the current version was installed. Calculate days difference to today.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use apt or dnf to display the installation date of the git platform package and compute days elapsed.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A log line with a date, e.g., '2024-01-10 install gitlab-ce'. Compare against current date to get days elapsed.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For GitLab, retrieve the current version via the API and then look up the release date from the GitLab releases API or package registry to compute days since update.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An ISO 8601 date string such as '2024-01-15T00:00:00.000Z'. Compute difference from today to determine days since last update.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For GitLab, navigate to the Admin Area to view the installed version, then cross-reference with the GitLab releases page to find the release date.
how_to_obtain.navigation: GitLab: Admin Area > Dashboard > Components section shows current version | Then visit: https://about.gitlab.com/releases/ to find the release date
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Version string displayed (e.g., '16.8.1') with corresponding release date on the public releases page, allowing manual computation of days elapsed.

typical_values: 180+ (critically outdated, high probability of known exploitable CVEs)

option_description: Indicates the network interface scope to which the Git service's web interface, SSH port, and API are bound. 'public' means bound to all interfaces (0.0.0.0 or ::), 'internal' means bound to a specific RFC1918/private network interface, and 'localhost' means bound only to the loopback adapter (127.0.0.1 or ::1).
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'network_exposure_to_untrusted_segments' when network_binding_scope is 'public' AND network_layer_control_present is false. A service bound to 0.0.0.0 without firewall controls is directly reachable from any network segment the host connects to, including the public internet. Given that the Git service holds source code, IaC definitions, and CI/CD pipeline secrets, public binding without compensating controls constitutes a critical attack surface exposure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use ss or netstat to inspect which interfaces the Git service ports are actually bound to on the host.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output like '0.0.0.0:3000' indicates public binding; '10.0.1.5:3000' indicates internal binding; '127.0.0.1:3000' indicates localhost-only binding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the Git service configuration file for the HTTP and SSH bind address settings.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Gitea: HTTP_ADDR = 0.0.0.0 (public), HTTP_ADDR = 10.0.0.1 (internal), or HTTP_ADDR = 127.0.0.1 (localhost). GitLab: external_url reflects the intended binding scope.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For GitLab, inspect the gitlab.rb and nginx configuration to determine interface binding.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines such as 'listen 0.0.0.0:80' (public) or 'listen 10.0.0.5:80' (internal) or 'listen 127.0.0.1:80' (localhost only).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt to connect to the Git service ports from an external or untrusted network perspective to confirm whether the binding scope results in actual reachability from untrusted segments.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: HTTP 200 or SSH banner received from an external test confirms public reachability. Connection timeout confirms non-public binding or firewall blocking.

typical_values: public (common in default installations without post-install hardening)
localhost (used when a reverse proxy handles external access)

option_description: Indicates whether at least one confirmed network-layer control — such as a firewall rule (iptables, ufw, cloud security group), VPN requirement, or reverse proxy with IP allowlisting — effectively restricts access to the Git service's ports from untrusted network segments.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires 'network_exposure_to_untrusted_segments' in two conditions: when network_binding_scope is 'public' AND network_layer_control_present is false, or when publicly_resolvable_hostname is true AND network_layer_control_present is false. The absence of network-layer controls means any network-reachable actor can reach authentication endpoints, SSH, and the API — dramatically expanding the attack surface for credential stuffing, vulnerability exploitation, and anonymous access abuse.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect iptables or nftables rules on the host to verify whether inbound access to Git service ports is restricted to known-good source IP ranges.
how_to_obtain.command: iptables -L INPUT -n -v --line-numbers | grep -E '3000|8080|443|80|22|2222' && nftables list ruleset 2>/dev/null | grep -E '3000|8080|443|22'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ACCEPT rules restricted to specific source IPs/CIDR ranges (e.g., 'source 10.0.0.0/8') confirm a network-layer control. Unrestricted ACCEPT or absence of rules confirms no control.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check ufw status to determine if a host-based firewall is active and restricting Git service ports.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Active ufw with rules like '3000/tcp ALLOW IN 10.0.0.0/8' confirms a network control. 'Status: inactive' or allow-all rules confirm absence of control.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For cloud-hosted deployments, query the cloud provider's API to retrieve the security group or firewall rules applied to the Git service host.
how_to_obtain.command: aws ec2 describe-security-groups --group-ids <sg-id> --query 'SecurityGroups[*].IpPermissions' --output json 2>/dev/null || gcloud compute firewall-rules list --filter='targetTags:<git-server-tag>' --format=json 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON showing inbound rules for ports 22, 80, 443, 3000. Rules limited to RFC1918 CIDR or specific corporate IP ranges confirm network-layer control. 0.0.0.0/0 source confirms absence.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify VPN enforcement by attempting to reach the Git service from a non-VPN connection and confirming a block, and from a VPN connection confirming access.
how_to_obtain.command: curl --max-time 5 --silent --output /dev/null --write-out '%{http_code}\n' https://<git-hostname>/ && echo 'Reachable without VPN — no VPN control confirmed'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Connection refused or timeout from non-VPN IP confirms VPN/firewall enforcement (network_layer_control_present = true). HTTP 200 without VPN confirms absence of control.

typical_values: false (common in default cloud VM deployments without security group hardening)
true (expected in production deployments behind corporate firewalls or VPN)

option_description: Indicates whether the Git service's configured external hostname resolves to a public (non-RFC1918, non-loopback) IP address when queried from an external DNS resolver, signaling that the service is intentionally or accidentally exposed to the public internet via DNS.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'network_exposure_to_untrusted_segments' when publicly_resolvable_hostname is true AND network_layer_control_present is false. A publicly resolvable hostname enables external threat actors to discover and target the service without prior knowledge of its IP address, effectively advertising the Git service's existence to internet-wide scanners (e.g., Shodan, Censys). This is particularly dangerous for a service aggregating source code, infrastructure configurations, and pipeline secrets.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Perform a DNS lookup of the configured Git service hostname using an external resolver to determine whether it resolves to a public IP address.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A public (non-RFC1918) IP address like '203.0.113.45' confirms publicly_resolvable_hostname = true. A private address (10.x, 172.16-31.x, 192.168.x) or NXDOMAIN confirms false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Extract the configured external hostname from the Git service configuration and test resolution in one pipeline.
how_to_obtain.command: EXT_URL=$(grep -E 'external_url|HTTP_DOMAIN|DOMAIN' /etc/gitlab/gitlab.rb /etc/gitea/app.ini 2>/dev/null | grep -oP 'https?://[^/"]+' | head -1 | sed 's|https\?://||'); echo "Testing: $EXT_URL"; dig "$EXT_URL" @8.8.8.8 +short | grep -vE '^(10\.|172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[01])\.|192\.168\.|127\.)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A non-empty public IP address output confirms publicly_resolvable_hostname = true. Empty output (all IPs are private or NXDOMAIN) confirms false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Identify the configured external URL or domain from the platform configuration file to determine the hostname to test.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A line like: external_url 'https://git.company.com' or ROOT_URL = https://git.internal.corp.com, providing the hostname to resolve externally.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use an internet-based DNS lookup service or API to check if the hostname resolves from outside the organization's network.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON with public IP addresses in the 'Answer' array confirms publicly_resolvable_hostname = true. Empty Answer array or NXDOMAIN in Status confirms false.

typical_values: true (common for SaaS-style internal tools accidentally exposed, or intentional public-facing instances)
false (expected for internal-only Git services using private DNS or split-horizon DNS)

option_description: Indicates whether the Git platform's on-disk configuration files — which contain database credentials, SMTP passwords, LDAP bind passwords, object storage access keys, and other secrets — are encrypted at rest rather than stored in plaintext. This includes integration with a secrets management backend such as HashiCorp Vault.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires 'secrets_stored_in_repository_configuration_or_history' when config_secrets_encrypted_at_rest is false (via 'not input.config_secrets_encrypted_at_rest'). Plaintext secrets in configuration files mean that any read access to the filesystem — achieved via path traversal, SSRF, backup exfiltration, or host compromise — immediately yields infrastructure-level credentials (database, LDAP, object storage). These credentials typically enable lateral movement far beyond the Git service itself.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the primary Git platform configuration file for plaintext credentials, looking for database passwords, SMTP credentials, LDAP bind passwords, and S3/object storage keys.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines showing plaintext values like: gitlab_rails['db_password'] = 'MyPlaintextPassword123' confirm config_secrets_encrypted_at_rest = false. References to Vault paths or ENC[] encrypted blobs suggest encryption is in use.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Gitea/Forgejo, inspect app.ini for plaintext database and external service credentials.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines like 'PASSWD = MyDBPassword' confirm plaintext storage (false). Empty output or references to secret manager integrations suggest encrypted or externalized secret storage.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for HashiCorp Vault integration or other secrets manager configuration that would indicate secrets are not stored in plaintext config files.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: References to Vault addresses, AWS Secrets Manager, or Azure Key Vault confirm an encrypted secrets backend is configured. Absence of any such references combined with plaintext values in config confirms false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check filesystem permissions and file metadata on configuration files to assess whether secrets are additionally protected by OS-level access controls, and verify if GitLab's secrets file exists and is populated.
how_to_obtain.command: ls -la /etc/gitlab/gitlab-secrets.json 2>/dev/null && python3 -c "import json,sys; d=json.load(open('/etc/gitlab/gitlab-secrets.json')); print('Keys present:', list(d.keys())[:5])" 2>/dev/null; stat /etc/gitea/app.ini 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'Access|Uid'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: GitLab's gitlab-secrets.json containing encrypted key material indicates secrets-at-rest protection for some values. File permissions of 600 owned by root/gitlab confirm restricted access, though this does not substitute for encryption.

typical_values: false (default for GitLab and Gitea installations — credentials written plaintext to config files out of the box)
true (achieved via Vault integration, encrypted secrets backends, or environment variable injection from a secrets manager)

option_description: Tracks whether a secret-scanning tool has found unrevoked credentials, API keys, tokens, or passwords in the current repository content or historical git commits (including all branches and tags). A true value indicates live or historical exposure of sensitive material that has not been purged or rewritten from the git history.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires the 'Secrets Stored In Repository Configuration Or History' exposure when secrets_detected_in_repository_commits is true AND secret_scanning_enabled is false. Even when scanning is enabled, the presence of detected-but-unrevoked secrets represents active credential exposure (MITRE T1552.001 Credentials In Files, T1213.003 Code Repositories). Because git history is immutable without explicit rewriting, a single historical commit containing an AWS access key or database password gives any repository reader infrastructure-level credentials, making this one of the highest-value findings in a self-hosted Git environment.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Run gitleaks against the full repository history, including all branches and tags, to detect any secrets present in commits. This must be run with full clone depth (not a shallow clone) to cover the entire history.
how_to_obtain.command: gitleaks detect --source /path/to/repo --log-opts='--all' --report-format json --report-path gitleaks-report.json; echo "Exit code: $?"; cat gitleaks-report.json | jq 'length'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Exit code 0 means no secrets detected (set attribute to false). Exit code 1 with findings in the JSON report means secrets were found (set attribute to true). Review the report to confirm findings are not false positives.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Run truffleHog as an alternative or supplementary scanner against the repository, scanning all git history with entropy and regex detection enabled.
how_to_obtain.command: trufflehog git file:///path/to/repo --json --only-verified 2>/dev/null | jq -s 'length'; trufflehog git file:///path/to/repo --json 2>/dev/null | jq -s '[.[] | select(.Verified == true)] | length'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A count greater than 0 for verified findings indicates secrets are present in history (set attribute to true). Zero verified findings suggests false, though unverified findings should still be reviewed.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For GitLab instances, navigate to the Security dashboard to review Secret Detection findings reported by pipeline scans. Check the vulnerability report filtered to 'Secret Detection' type across all projects.
how_to_obtain.navigation: GitLab Admin Area > Security > Vulnerability Report > Filter by 'Secret Detection' > Review all 'Critical' and 'High' severity findings. Also check: Project > Security & Compliance > Vulnerability Report for each repository.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any active (unresolved) Secret Detection vulnerabilities with status 'Detected' or 'Confirmed' indicate secrets_detected_in_repository_commits should be set to true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query GitLab's Vulnerability API to programmatically retrieve all secret detection findings across repositories, filtering for unresolved findings.
how_to_obtain.command: curl --header 'PRIVATE-TOKEN: <admin_token>' 'https://<gitlab-host>/api/v4/vulnerabilities?state=detected&scanner_id=secrets&per_page=100' | jq '[.[] | {id, project: .project.name, title, severity, state}]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A non-empty JSON array indicates active secret detection findings exist (set attribute to true). An empty array [] suggests no platform-reported secrets, but still validate with gitleaks/truffleHog for full coverage.

typical_values: true — Common in organizations without established secret hygiene; historical commits frequently contain database credentials, cloud provider keys, and internal API tokens committed during development.
false — Achieved only when scanning confirms no secrets in current files or history, or when history has been rewritten (git filter-repo) and all detected secrets have been revoked and rotated.

option_description: Indicates whether automated secret scanning is configured to detect credentials before or immediately after they are committed. This includes pre-receive hooks that block pushes containing secrets, CI/CD pipeline steps that scan each commit, or platform-native secret detection features (such as GitLab Secret Detection SAST or GitHub Advanced Security) that run on every push and pull request.
security_impact: The Rego policy evaluates secret_scanning_enabled as a paired condition with secrets_detected_in_repository_commits: exposure is triggered when secrets are present AND scanning is not enabled. Beyond the paired rule, the absence of scanning (false) represents a systematic control gap — without automated detection, developers have no immediate feedback loop to prevent secret commits, meaning secrets can persist in history indefinitely (MITRE T1552 Unsecured Credentials, T1552.001 Credentials In Files). Pre-receive hooks provide the strongest preventive control by blocking commits at push time; pipeline scanning and platform-native detection provide detective controls. At least one layer must be active for this attribute to be set to true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For GitLab, check whether Secret Detection is enabled in the Security Configuration of each project and verify the platform-level default pipeline includes the secret detection template. For Gitea or Forgejo, check if pre-receive hooks are installed at the server level.
how_to_obtain.navigation: GitLab: Project > Security & Compliance > Security Configuration > 'Secret Detection' row — must show 'Enabled'. Also check: Admin Area > CI/CD > Default pipeline configuration for inclusion of 'Security/Secret-Detection.gitlab-ci.yml' template. Gitea: Site Administration > Git Hooks > pre-receive hook contents.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: GitLab showing 'Enabled' with a green checkmark for Secret Detection, or a pre-receive hook script that invokes gitleaks or truffleHog on each push, indicates secret_scanning_enabled should be set to true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the GitLab CI/CD pipeline configuration files for inclusion of the secret detection job, or check server-side git hook scripts deployed to the git repositories' hooks directory.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Finding references to Secret-Detection templates in CI config, or a pre-receive hook script calling a scanner binary, confirms scanning is enabled (true). Missing hooks directory or empty hook files confirms false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the GitLab API to check whether Secret Detection jobs appear in recent pipeline runs for a representative set of repositories, confirming the scanner actually executes on push.
how_to_obtain.command: curl --header 'PRIVATE-TOKEN: <admin_token>' 'https://<gitlab-host>/api/v4/projects/<project_id>/pipelines?per_page=5' | jq '.[].id' | while read pid; do curl --header 'PRIVATE-TOKEN: <admin_token>' "https://<gitlab-host>/api/v4/projects/<project_id>/pipelines/$pid/jobs" | jq '[.[] | select(.name | test("secret|Secret"))] | {pipeline: '$pid', secret_jobs: .}'; done
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON output showing jobs with names containing 'secret' or 'Secret Detection' in recent pipeline runs confirms scanning is active (true). No matching jobs across multiple recent pipelines indicates secret_scanning_enabled should be set to false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the platform administrator or review the Git service onboarding documentation to determine whether a policy mandates secret scanning on all repositories, and whether enforcement is verified through compliance checks or pipeline enforcement rules.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Request documentation of: (1) the CI/CD template repository enforcing secret scanning inclusion, (2) any GitLab Compliance Framework or Pipeline Execution Policy that injects secret detection into all pipelines, (3) evidence of pre-receive hook deployment runbooks or Ansible/Chef/Puppet automation that installs hooks on repository creation.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Existence of enforced compliance pipeline policies, documented runbooks for hook deployment, or a compliance framework enforcing the secret detection template across all projects supports setting the attribute to true. Absence of any such documentation or policy means the default is likely false.

typical_values: false — The most common state in self-hosted Git deployments without a mature DevSecOps program; pre-receive hooks are rarely deployed by default, and optional CI templates are frequently omitted from project pipelines.

true — Achieved in organizations using GitLab Ultimate with enforced Compliance Pipelines, or with centrally managed pre-receive hooks deployed via configuration management tools; requires active enforcement rather than optional enablement.
